claim: Eya1-/- embryos at E9.5 showed hypoplastic second and third pharyngeal arches with barely visible pharyngeal clefts.
source: In contrast, at E9.5, Eya1-/- embryos showed hypoplastic second and third PA with barely visible pharyngeal clefts (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in whole mount embryos shown in Figure 1B and C, comparing wildtype and Eya1-/- embryos.

claim: In Eya1-/- embryos, pharyngeal segmental plates were not formed.
source: E-cadherin immunostaining, which labeled the ectodermal and endodermal epithelia, revealed that the pharyngeal segmental plates were not formed.
evidence: Supported by E-cadherin immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: In Eya1-/- embryos, there were no contact points between the pharyngeal ectoderm and endoderm-derived epithelia.
source: There were no contact points between the pharyngeal ectoderm and endoderm-derived epithelia, such that the pharyngeal clefts and pouches could not form properly and the pharyngeal mesenchyme in adjacent PA never separated (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by E-cadherin immunostaining shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: In E10 Eya1-/- embryos, PA2 was shortened with an apparent reduction of the proximal portion while the distal part was still present.
source: In E10 Eya1-/- embryos the PA2 was shortened, with an apparent reduction of the proximal portion, while the distal part was still present (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by scanning electron microscopy images in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Dlx1 expression was lost in the proximal portion of the pharyngeal arch but retained in the distal arches in Eya1-/- embryos at E9.5.
source: At E9.5, Dlx1 expression was lost in the Eya1-/- embryos in the proximal portion of the PA, but retained in the distal arches (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: Dlx5 was expressed in the distal region in both wildtype and Eya1-/- embryos at E9.5.
source: Dlx5 was expressed in the distal region in both wildtype and Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 1L and M)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Brn1 expression was lost in proximal PA2 in Eya1-/- embryos but expressed in the maxillary-mandibular junction of PA1 and proximal region of PA2 in wildtype.
source: whereas Brn1 expression was lost in proximal PA2 in Eya1-/- embryos but expressed in the maxillary-mandibular junction of PA1 and proximal region of PA2 in wildtype (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1N and O.

claim: The migrating neural crest stream in PA2 was reduced in Eya1-/- embryos.
source: We examined the expression of the neural crest marker gene Crabp1 and confirmed that the migrating neural crest stream in the PA2 was reduced in the Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by Crabp1 in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Eya1-/- embryos displayed increased cell death at the dorsal level around the entrances of PA1 and PA2.
source: TUNEL analysis revealed that the Eya1-/- embryos displayed increased cell death at the dorsal level around the entrances of PA1 and PA2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1E).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1E.

claim: At E8.5, Eya1 was expressed broadly in the posterior placode and the pharyngeal region, including the pharyngeal ectoderm and pharyngeal pouch.
source: At E8.5 and before the pharyngeal arch outgrowth, Eya1 was expressed broadly in the posterior placode and the pharyngeal region, including the pharyngeal ectoderm and pharyngeal pouch (Figure 2A and A').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and A'.

claim: At E9.5, Eya1 was restricted to the maxillary and most distal part of PA1, the proximal-rostral and caudal parts of PA2, and the posterior PA.
source: At E9.5, Eya1 was restricted to the maxillary and most distal part of PA1, the proximal-rostral and caudal parts of PA2, and the posterior PA (Figure 2B and B').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B and B'.

claim: Eya1 immunoreactivity was observed in both cytoplasm and nucleus in ectodermal cells.
source: Eya1 immunoreactivity was observed in both cytoplasm and nucleus in ectodermal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and A').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and A'.

claim: The expression pattern of Six1 was similar to Eya1 at E9.5.
source: The expression pattern of Six1 was similar to Eya1 at E9.5 (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Six1 expression extended into the pharyngeal ectomesenchyme at E9.5.
source: although Six1 expression also extended into the pharyngeal ectomesenchyme (Figure 2C').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C'.

claim: Sox2+ cells were still observed in the pharyngeal ectoderm in both Eya1-/- and Six1-/- mutants.
source: However, Sox2+ cells were still observed in the pharyngeal ectoderm in both mutants (Figure 2D–2F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D–2F.

claim: In Eya1-/- embryos, Sox2+ cells were found in the residual proximal pharyngeal ectoderm, and the total number of Sox2+ cells in the mutant geniculate placode (139 ± 33, n = 3) was significantly reduced compared with wildtype (286 ± 26, n = 3).
source: In Eya1-/- embryos, Sox2+ cells were found in the residual proximal pharyngeal ectoderm, and the total number of Sox2+ cells in the mutant geniculate placode (139 ± 33, n = 3) was significantly reduced compared with wildtype (286 ± 26, n = 3).
evidence: Supported by quantification of Sox2+ cells in immunostaining experiments.

claim: Expression of Sox3 was reduced in Eya1-/- embryos but unaffected in Six1-/- ectoderm.
source: Expression of Sox3, which also regulates pharyngeal segmentation and proximal PA2 development (Rizzoti and Lovell-Badge, 2007), was reduced in Eya1-/- (Figure 2H) but unaffected in Six1-/- ectoderm (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2H and I, with citation to prior work.

claim: In wildtype and Six1-/- E9.5 embryos, Fgf3 expression was observed in the rostral-proximal pharyngeal ectoderm and endoderm.
source: In wildtype and Six1-/- E9.5 embryos, Fgf3 expression was observed in the rostral-proximal pharyngeal ectoderm and endoderm (Figure 2M, M, O and O').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2M, M, O and O'.

claim: Fgf3 expression in the pharyngeal endoderm was retained in the Eya1-/- embryos.
source: While Fgf3 expression in the pharyngeal endoderm was retained in the Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 2N')
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2N'.

claim: Fgf3 expression was dramatically reduced in the Sox2+ epithelial cells in Eya1-/- embryos.
source: Fgf3 expression was dramatically reduced in the Sox2+ epithelial cells (Figure 2N and N').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2N and N'.

claim: Expression of Fgf15 and Fgf8 was reduced in the Eya1-/- embryos, but unaffected in the Six1-/- embryos.
source: Expression of Fgf15 and Fgf8 was also reduced in the Eya1-/- embryos, but unaffected in the Six1-/- embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–1G).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–1G.

claim: The expression of Fgfr1 was neither affected in the Eya1-/- nor in the Six1-/- embryos.
source: In contrast, the expression of Fgfr1 was neither affected in the Eya1-/- nor in the Six1-/- embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–1J).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–1J.

claim: Spry1 expression in the ectoderm was specifically downregulated in Eya1-/- embryos but not in Six1-/- embryos.
source: Spry1 expression in the ectoderm was specifically downregulated in Eya1-/- embryos but not in Six1-/- embryos (Figure 2P–2R')
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2P–2R'.

claim: Pharyngeal arch segmentation occurred normally in the Six1-/- embryos.
source: Pharyngeal arch segmentation occurred normally in the Six1-/- embryos (Figure 2F, I, L', O' and and R')
evidence: Supported by multiple markers shown in Figure 2F, I, L', O' and R'.

claim: Epibranchial placodal cells in the Eya1-/- embryos did not express Neurog2.
source: Finally, epibranchial placodal cells in the Eya1-/- embryos did not express Neurog2 (Figure 2T and T')
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2T and T'.

claim: Neurog2 expression was still observed in the petrosal and nodose placodes in the Six1-/- embryos.
source: while Neurog2 expression was still observed in the petrosal and nodose placodes in the Six1-/- embryos (Figure 2U and U').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2U and U'.

claim: At E8.0 (5 somites), the thickened placodal ectoderm was Sox2+ and none of the cells was Fgf3+ or Neurog2+.
source: At E8.0 (5ss), the thickened placodal ectoderm was Sox2+ and none of the cells was Fgf3+ or Neurog2+ (Figure 3A and F–G').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and F–G'.

claim: At E8.5 (8 somites), Neurog2 and Fgf3 expression started to emerge in the Sox2+ placodal ectoderm.
source: At E8.5 (8ss), Neurog2 and Fgf3 expression started to emerge in the Sox2+ placodal ectoderm (Figure 3B and I–J').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B and I–J'.

claim: Co-staining for Sox2 and Neurog2 showed a salt-and-pepper expression distribution at 15 somites.
source: Co-staining for Sox2 and Neurog2 showed a salt-and-pepper expression distribution at 15ss (Figure 3L)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: At 15 somites, three types of expression patterns could be discerned: Sox2 single positive, Neurog2 single positive, and Sox2/Neurog2 double positive cells.
source: and three types of expression patterns could be discerned: Sox2 single positive, Neurog2 single positive, and Sox2/Neurog2 double positive cells.
evidence: Inferred from the salt-and-pepper distribution observed in immunostaining.

claim: Fgf3 expression could be detected in the Sox2+ cell population at 15 somites.
source: Fgf3 expression could also be detected in the Sox2+ cell population (Figure 3C and M–M').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C and M–M'.

claim: At 8-15 somites, there were Fgf3/Sox2 double positive cells in the Neurog2 positive region.
source: At 8-15ss, there were Fgf3/Sox2 double positive cells in the Neurog2 positive region (Figure 3I–3J' and and L–M').
evidence: Supported by co-staining data shown in Figure 3I–3J' and L–M'.

claim: At E9.5 (25 somites), all Neurog2+ cells were sorted to the proximal region while the Sox2+/Fgf3+ cells were confined to the more distal region on the lateral surface of the PA.
source: Interestingly, at E9.5 (25ss), all Neurog2+ cells were sorted to the proximal region while the Sox2+/Fgf3+ cells were confined to the more distal region on the lateral surface of the PA (Figure 3O–3P').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3O–3P'.

claim: Eya1 was co-expressed with Sox2 from 5 somites onwards and was expressed in both the Neurog2+ and Fgf3+ regions from 8 to 25 somites.
source: Eya1 was co-expressed with Sox2 from 5ss onwards and was expressed in both the Neurog2+ and Fgf3+ regions from 8 to 25ss (Figure 3E, H, K and N).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E, H, K and N.

claim: The Fgf3+/Sox2+/Neurog2- cells define a new non-neuronal cell lineage in the epibranchial placode.
source: Since the Fgf3+/Sox2+/Neurog2- cells also exhibited a thickened epithelial morphology and expressed Eya1, we propose that these cells define a new non-neuronal cell lineage in the epibranchial placode.
evidence: Based on morphological and molecular marker analysis of these cells.

claim: In Eya1-/- embryos, Neurog2 expression was lost while Sox2 expression was still retained in the epithelium from E8.0 to E9.5.
source: In Eya1-/- embryos, Neurog2 expression was lost while Sox2 expression was still retained in the epithelium from E8.0 to E9.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1D').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1D'.

claim: While the Neurog2+ neurogenic placodal cells were lost, the Sox2+ cells in the non-neuronal lineage remained in the Eya1-/- embryos.
source: Therefore, while the Neurog2+ neurogenic placodal cells were lost, the Sox2+ cells in the non-neuronal lineage remained in the Eya1-/- embryos (depicted in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sox2 expression persists while Neurog2 is lost.

claim: Tamoxifen induction at E7.5 in Sox2-CreER; R26REYFP mice labeled Sox2-expressing cells, and some EYFP-expressing cells at E9.5 were also positive for Islet1, a marker for delaminating neurons.
source: Analysis of tamoxifen-injected embryos two days later, at E9.5 (Figure 3Q), revealed that some EYFP-expressing cells were also positive for Islet1, a marker for delaminating neurons (Figure 3R)
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3Q and R.

claim: EYFP-expression was observed in cells with thickened epithelial morphology, which expressed Sox2 and also gave rise to the pharyngeal cleft, and proximal pharyngeal ectoderm cells.
source: We however also observed EYFP-expression in cells with thickened epithelial morphology, which expressed Sox2 and also gave rise to the pharyngeal cleft, and proximal pharyngeal ectoderm cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3S).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3S.

claim: Cells expressing Sox2 at E7.5 segregated to delaminating neurons as well as to cells in the non-neurogenic lineage.
source: This indicates that cells expressing Sox2 at E7.5 segregated to delaminating neurons as well as to cells in the non-neurogenic lineage.
evidence: Inferred from lineage tracing experiments showing both neuronal and non-neuronal fates.

claim: By injection of tamoxifen at E9.5 and analysis at E12.5 and E14.5, EYFP expression was detected in the external auditory canal and pinna epithelium, indicating that non-neuronal cells were produced.
source: By injection of tamoxifen at E9.5 and analysis at E12.5 and E14.5, we detected EYFP expression in the external auditory canal and pinna epithelium, indicating that non-neuronal cells were produced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: The pharyngeal ectoderm showed extensive co-expression of Notch1 with Eya1 and Sox2 from E8.0 onwards.
source: The pharyngeal ectoderm showed extensive co-expression of Notch1 with Eya1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–1A'') and Sox2 from E8.0 onwards (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O and Q).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–1A'', O and Q.

claim: Notch immunoreactivity was observed in the nuclei, indicating active Notch signaling.
source: Notch immunoreactivity was observed also in the nuclei, indicating active Notch signaling
evidence: Nuclear localization of Notch is a hallmark of active signaling.

claim: Hey1, a Notch downstream target, was expressed at the pharyngeal ectoderm, with a distribution similar to that of Sox2 from E8.5 to E9.5.
source: a notion further supported by expression of Hey1, a Notch downstream target, at the pharyngeal ectoderm, with a distribution similar to that of Sox2 from E8.5 to E9.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–1E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–1E.

claim: The expression domain of the Notch ligand Delta-like1 (Dll1) overlapped with that of Neurog2 from E8.5 to E9.5.
source: In contrast, the expression domain of the Notch ligand Delta-like1 (Dll1) was found to overlap with that of Neurog2 from E8.5 to E9.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–1I).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–1I.

claim: The expression domain of the Jag1 (Jagged1) ligand was broader and extended across both the Neurog2+ and Fgf3+ regions.
source: The expression domain of the Jag1 (Jagged1) ligand was broader, extended across both the Neurog2+ and Fgf3+ regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–M.

claim: In wildtype embryos, V1744 immunoreactivity was observed in the ectodermal and endodermal cells as well as in the neural crest.
source: In wildtype embryos, V1744 immunoreactivity was observed in the ectodermal and endodermal cells as well as in the neural crest (Figure 4A and A')
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and A'.

claim: The ectodermal V1744 staining was specifically lost in the Eya1-/- embryos.
source: whereas the ectodermal staining was specifically lost in the Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 4B and B').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B and B'.

claim: The C20 immunoreactivity revealed a specific reduction of Notch1 immunoreactivity in the rostral-proximal ectodermal cells in Eya1-/- embryos.
source: The C20 immunoreactivity revealed a specific reduction of Notch1 immunoreactivity in the rostral-proximal ectodermal cells (Figure 4D and D') as compared to wildtype (Figure 4C and C')
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C, C', D and D'.

claim: Notch1 mRNA was expressed in the ectodermal cells at E8.5 (8 somites) and E9.5.
source: By in situ hybridization, we found that Notch1 mRNA was expressed in the ectodermal cells at E8.5 (8ss) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1S and T) and E9.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1U and V)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1S, T, U and V.

claim: Notch1 protein expression was reduced from around 8 somites in the Sox2+ placodal progenitors in Eya1-/- embryos, indicating post-transcriptional regulation of Notch1.
source: while the protein expression of Notch1 was reduced from around 8ss in the Sox2+ placodal progenitors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O–1R'), indicating post-transcriptional regulation of Notch1 in Eya1-/- embryos.
evidence: Supported by comparison of mRNA and protein expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Notch3 receptor, which was expressed in the pharyngeal ectoderm, was not affected in the Eya1-/- embryos.
source: The Notch3 receptor, which was also expressed in the pharyngeal ectoderm, was not affected in the Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1X').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1X'.

claim: In wildtype embryos, Jag1 was expressed at high level at the PA segmental plate contact points and at a lower level in the rostral-proximal ectoderm; similar expression pattern was found in Eya1-/- embryos despite the absence of PA segmental plates.
source: In wildtype embryos, Jag1 was expressed at high level at the PA segmental plate contact points and at a lower level in the rostral-proximal ectoderm, similar expression pattern was found in Eya1-/- embryos despite the absence of PA segmental plates (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Dll1 expression was lost in the epibranchial placode region in Eya1-/- embryos.
source: On the other hand, Dll1 expression was lost in the epibranchial placode region in Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The downregulation of total amount of Notch1 protein was confirmed by Western blot analysis of dissected pharyngeal regions from E9.5 Eya1-/- embryos.
source: The downregulation of total amount of Notch1 protein was confirmed by Western blot analysis of dissected pharyngeal regions from E9.5 Eya1-/- embryos, and Eya1 protein levels were as expected non-detectable (Figure 4M).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: Expression of Hey1 was significantly downregulated in the ectoderm in the Eya1-/- E9.5 embryos.
source: In keeping with reduced Notch1 receptor levels, expression of Hey1 was significantly downregulated in the ectoderm in the Eya1-/- E9.5 embryos (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Expression of Hes1 was much less affected in Eya1-/- embryos.
source: Expression of Hes1, however, was much less affected (Figure 4K and L)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4K and L.

claim: Substantial Hes1 expression was observed in RBPJ-/- embryos, suggesting that Hes1 is also regulated by other factors.
source: which is consistent with that substantial Hes1 expression was observed in RBPJ-/- embryos (de la Pompa et al., 1997), suggesting that Hes1 is also regulated by other factors.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work showing Hes1 expression in RBPJ-/- embryos.

claim: Cre activity and ectopic Notch1 ICD expression in Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC embryos were revealed by EYFP and GFP staining, respectively, and were both observed in the pharyngeal ectoderm.
source: Cre activity and ectopic Notch1 ICD expression were revealed by EYFP and GFP staining, respectively (Figure 5A and C), and were both observed in the pharyngeal ectoderm (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5A, B, C and D.

claim: A definitive first pharyngeal cleft could be found in the Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos.
source: A definitive first pharyngeal cleft could be found in the Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 5F), compared with the defective pharyngeal cleft in Eya1-/-embryos (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by whole mount imaging data shown in Figure 5F and comparison to Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of Hey1 confirmed the upregulation of Notch signaling in the Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC and Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos.
source: Expression of Hey1 confirmed the upregulation of Notch signaling in the Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC and Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Using B2-r4-Cre and Sox2-CreER drivers to express Notch1 ICD, the pharyngeal segmentation phenotype was restored in Eya1-/- embryos.
source: To corroborate the restoration of pharyngeal cleft by elevating Notch signaling, we used two other Cre drivers (B2-r4-Cre and Sox2-CreER) (Szeto et al., 2009; Arnold et al., 2011) to express Notch1 ICD, and in both cases the pharyngeal segmentation phenotype was restored in Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: Supported by whole mount imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–J, with citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of Notch1 ICD from the Pax2-Cre driver in a wildtype background did not affect the normal pharyngeal cleft formation.
source: Moreover, expression of Notch1 ICD from the Pax2-Cre driver in a wildtype background, i.e. elevating Notch signaling above the normal level rather than restoring reduced Notch signaling, did not affect the normal pharyngeal cleft formation (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by whole mount imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Immunostaining of E-cadherin showed that in E9.5 compound mutants (Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/-) the pharyngeal ectoderm and endoderm made contacts and proper pharyngeal arch segmentation took place.
source: To analyze the rescued phenotype in further detail, immunostaining of E-cadherin to mark the epithelium showed that in E9.5 compound mutants the pharyngeal ectoderm and endoderm made contacts and proper pharyngeal arch segmentation took place (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Brn1 expression was restored in the maxillary-mandibular junction of PA1 and proximal PA2 in Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos.
source: Brn1 expression was also restored in the maxillary-mandibular junction of PA1 and proximal PA2 in Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 5N and N').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5N and N'.

claim: An increased number of Sox2+ progenitors could be observed in the entire ectodermal epithelium of PA2 of the Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC and Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- embryos.
source: An increased number of Sox2+ progenitors could be observed in the entire ectodermal epithelium of PA2 of the Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC and Pax2-Cre; Rosa26N1-IC; Eya1-/- (Figure 5R and R').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5R and R'.

claim: Pax2-Cre mediated Notch1 ICD expression rescued the expression of Fgf3 at E9.5.
source: Furthermore, Pax2-Cre mediated Notch1 ICD expression rescued the expression of Fgf3 at E9.5 (Figure 5V and V').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5V and V'.

claim: The reduced expression of Spry1 in the Eya1-/- embryos was restored upon Notch1 ICD expression.
source: The reduced expression of Spry1 in the Eya1-/- embryos (Figure 2Q) was restored upon Notch1 ICD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Neurog2 expression was inhibited by Notch1 ICD expression.
source: Importantly, however, Neurog2 expression was inhibited by Notch1 ICD expression (Figure 5Y and Z)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5Y and Z.

claim: Induced Notch signaling can restore Fgf downstream signaling, rescue the morphological and functional defects of pharyngeal epithelium caused by loss of Eya1.
source: Collectively, the results indicate that induced Notch signaling can restore Fgf downstream signaling, rescue the morphological and functional defects of pharyngeal epithelium caused by loss of Eya1
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing restoration of multiple phenotypes.

claim: Notch signaling is sufficient to promote the formation of the non-neurogenic epibranchial cell population.
source: and that Notch signaling is sufficient to promote the formation of the non-neurogenic epibranchial cell population.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of Sox2+/Fgf3+ cells and inhibition of Neurog2 by Notch1 ICD.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed an interaction between Flag-Eya1 and Myc-Notch1 ICD.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments revealed an interaction between Flag-Eya1 and Myc-Notch1 ICD (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Eya1 showed a strong interaction with Myc-Notch1 ICD while the N-terminal domain exhibited a very weak or no interaction.
source: and the C-terminal domain of Eya1 showed a strong interaction with Myc-Notch1 ICD while the N-terminal domain exhibited a very weak or no interaction (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Co-transfected cells with a constant amount of Myc-Notch1 ICD and increasing amounts of Flag-Eya1 showed that the amount of Notch1 ICD was elevated proportionally to the increase in the amount of Eya1.
source: Furthermore, co-transfected cells with a constant amount of Myc-Notch1 ICD and increasing amounts of Flag-Eya1 showed that the amount of Notch1 ICD was elevated proportionally to the increase in the amount of Eya1 (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Eya1 enhances the stability of Notch1 ICD.
source: suggesting that Eya1 enhances the stability of Notch1 ICD.
evidence: Inferred from the dose-dependent increase in Notch1 ICD levels with Eya1.

claim: Increased amounts of full length Notch1 receptor and a membrane-tethered form mimicking an ADAM-processed Notch1 receptor (Notch1ΔE) were observed in response to Eya1 in cells treated with γ-secretase inhibitor (DAPT).
source: We also observed increased amounts of full length Notch1 receptor and a membrane-tethered form mimicking an ADAM-processed Notch1 receptor (Notch1ΔE) in response to Eya1 in cells that were treated with γ-secretase inhibitor (DAPT) to block S3-mediated cleavage of the receptor (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The short half-life of Notch1 ICD (approximately 5 hr) was significantly extended (more than 10 hr) when Eya1 was co-transfected.
source: To assess the half-life of Notch1 ICD, we blocked protein synthesis by cycloheximide, and the short half-life of Notch1 ICD (approximately 5 hr), which is in keeping with previous reports (Gustafsson et al., 2005), was significantly extended (more than 10 hr) when Eya1 was co-transfected (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6E and F, with citation to prior work.

claim: Two Eya1 mutants DYY and Y4, which largely affect the threonine phosphatase activity, did not stabilize Notch1 ICD.
source: In contrast to the prolongation of Notch1 ICD half-life by wildtype Eya1, two Eya1 mutants DYY and Y4, which largely affect the threonine phosphatase activity (Okabe et al., 2009) did not stabilize Notch1 ICD (Figure 6E and F)
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6E and F, with citation to prior work.

claim: Eya1D327N, which affects both the tyrosine and threonine phosphatase activities, did not stabilize Notch1 ICD.
source: and this was the case also for Eya1D327N, which affects both the tyrosine and threonine phosphatase activities (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the cycloheximide chase experiments, with citation to prior work.

claim: In the presence of Eya1, the total amount of Notch1 ICD was increased but the amount of threonine-phosphorylated Notch1 ICD was reduced.
source: Analysis using anti-phosphopeptide-specific antibodies for threonine, serine and tyrosine revealed that in the presence of Eya1, the total amount of Notch1 ICD was increased but the amount of threonine-phosphorylated Notch1 ICD was reduced (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The serine-phosphorylated Notch1 ICD was not affected by Eya1.
source: In contrast, the serine-phosphorylated Notch1 ICD was not affected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tyrosine-phosphorylated Notch ICD was hardly detected.
source: and tyrosine-phosphorylated Notch ICD was hardly detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In vitro phosphatase experiments showed that in the presence of Eya1 the amount of threonine-phosphorylated Notch1 ICD was reduced.
source: In keeping with these data, in vitro phosphatase experiments, using purified Flag-Eya1 and Flag-Notch1 ICD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), showed that in the presence of Eya1 the amount of threonine-phosphorylated Notch1 ICD was reduced (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The ubiquitinated-Notch1 ICD level was enhanced by Fbw7, but reduced significantly in the presence of Eya1.
source: By immunoprecipitation experiments, we demonstrated that the ubiquitinated-Notch1 ICD level was enhanced by Fbw7, but reduced significantly in the presence of Eya1 (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The level of ubiquitination, assessed by anti-HA antibody, was reduced by Eya1.
source: The level of ubiquitination, assessed by anti-HA antibody, was also reduced by Eya1 (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Eya1 interacts with Notch1 ICD via its C-terminal domain.
source: In conclusion, the data show that Eya1 interacts with Notch1 ICD via its C-terminal domain
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing interaction with C-terminal domain.

claim: Eya1 acts as a threonine phosphatase on Notch1 ICD, controlling its stability.
source: and that Eya1 acts as a threonine phosphatase on Notch1 ICD, controlling its stability.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing dephosphorylation and stabilization of Notch1 ICD by Eya1.

claim: There is a sequence similarity between the region around T2122 in Notch1 ICD and the region neighboring T58 in c-Myc.
source: To identify the target dephosphorylated threonine residue on Notch1 ICD, we noted that there was a sequence similarity between the region around T2122 in Notch1 ICD and the region neighboring T58 in c-Myc (Wei et al., 2005) (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A, with citation to prior work.

claim: T58 in c-Myc is an established target threonine residue for the Eya1 threonine phosphatase activity.
source: an established target threonine residue for the Eya1 threonine phosphatase activity (Xu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The phospho-dead Notch1 ICDT2122A mutant could interact with Eya1.
source: The phospho-dead Notch1 ICDT2122A mutant could interact with Eya1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The threonine phosphorylation status of Notch1 ICDT2122A was not altered by Eya1, indicating that T2122 is the phosphorylation site targeted by Eya1.
source: and its threonine phosphorylation status was not altered by Eya1 (Figure 7B), indicating that T2122 is the phosphorylation site targeted by Eya1.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The amount and threonine phosphorylation of in vitro phosphorylated Notch1 ICDT2122A was largely unaffected by Eya1.
source: In line with this, the amount and threonine phosphorylation of in vitro phosphorylated Notch1 ICDT2122A was largely unaffected by Eya1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: T2487 in Notch1 ICD was not affected by Eya1 and therefore unlikely to be an in vivo target.
source: The only other candidate site for Eya1 phosphatase activity in Notch1 ICD (T2487) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), which is also a target of Fbw7 (O'Neil et al., 2007), was not affected by Eya1 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) and therefore unlikely to be an in vivo target.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, with citation to prior work.

claim: The phospho-dead Notch1 ICDT2122A was considerably more stable (half-life = 10 hr) than control Notch1 ICD.
source: The results from the cycloheximide treatment experiments showed that the phospho-dead Notch1 ICDT2122A was considerably more stable (half-life = 10 hr) than control Notch1 ICD
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Eya1 did not significantly alter the stability of Notch1 ICDT2122A.
source: whereas Eya1 did not significantly alter the stability of Notch1 ICDT2122A (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The phospho-mimetic Notch1 ICDT2122D mutant displayed a short half-life (5 hr), at par with control Notch1 ICD, and its half-life was not affected by Eya1.
source: In contrast, the phospho-mimetic Notch1 ICDT2122D mutant displayed a short half-life (5 hr), at par with control Notch1 ICD, and its half-life was not affected by Eya1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Threonine 2122 plays a crucial role in regulating Notch1 ICD stability and is the likely target amino acid residue for the threonine phosphatase activity of Eya1.
source: In sum, these results show that threonine 2122 plays a crucial role in regulating Notch1 ICD stability and is the likely target amino acid residue for the threonine phosphatase activity of Eya1.
evidence: Inferred from the mutational analysis showing that T2122 mutations affect stability and Eya1 responsiveness.

claim: Epibranchial placodes contain bipotential epithelial progenitors that produce a non-neuronal cell lineage important for pharyngeal arch development.
source: We also provide evidence that epibranchial placodes are not limited to generating viscero-sensory neurons only, but contain bipotential epithelial progenitors that in addition produce a non-neuronal cell lineage important for PA development.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing and marker analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Notch1 ICD is a novel target of the threonine phosphatase activity of Eya1.
source: We further identified Notch1 ICD as a novel target of the threonine phosphatase activity of Eya1.
evidence: Supported by multiple biochemical experiments showing dephosphorylation of Notch1 ICD by Eya1.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Notch1 ICD leads to stabilization of Notch1 ICD and enhanced Notch signaling.
source: Dephosphorylation leads to stabilization of Notch1 ICD and enhanced Notch signaling.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing increased Notch1 ICD stability and downstream target expression upon Eya1 expression.

claim: An Eya1-Notch axis is important for pharyngeal arch formation and craniofacial morphogenesis.
source: Our data provide evidence for a more complex composition of epibranchial placodes and an Eya1-Notch axis important for PA formation and craniofacial morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by genetic and biochemical experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in the human EYA1 and SIX genes, including SIX1 and SIX5, are reported in approximately 50% of the patients suffering from Branchio-Oto-Renal (BOR) syndrome.
source: The importance of Eya and Six proteins for craniofacial development is underscored by that mutations in the human EYA1 and SIX genes, including SIX1 and SIX5, are reported in approximately 50% of the patients suffering from Branchio-Oto-Renal (BOR) syndrome (Abdelhak et al., 1997; Smith, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Eya1 mutant mouse embryos display phenotypes in multiple pharyngeal and placodal derivatives including cranial neural crest cell-derived bones and cartilages, endoderm-derived tympanic cavity, thymus, thyroid and parathyroid glands, ectoderm-derived external auditory canal, otic and epibranchial placodes.
source: Eya1 mutant mouse embryos display phenotypes in multiple pharyngeal and placodal derivatives including cranial neural crest cell-derived bones and cartilages, endoderm-derived tympanic cavity, thymus, thyroid and parathyroid glands, ectoderm-derived external auditory canal, otic and epibranchial placodes (Xu et al., 1999, 2002; Zou et al., 2004, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Six1-/- and Six4-/- mouse embryos exhibit pharyngeal phenotypes along with kidney problems.
source: Six1-/- and Six4-/- mouse embryos also exhibit pharyngeal phenotypes along with kidney problems (Laclef et al., 2003; Zou et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The tyrosine phosphatase activity of Eya1 regulates H2AX and DNA repair.
source: The tyrosine phosphatase activity of Eya1 regulates H2AX and DNA repair (Cook et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The tyrosine phosphatase activity of Eya1 is required for the function of Eya1 as a transactivator in conjunction with Six.
source: and is also required for the function of Eya1 as a transactivator in conjunction with Six (Li et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dephosphorylation of T58 in c-Myc by Eya1 is important for nephrogenesis and tumour growth.
source: Less is known about the threonine phosphatase activity, but dephosphorylation of T58 in c-Myc by Eya1 has been shown to be important for nephrogenesis and tumour growth (Xu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of Notch results in proximal pharyngeal arch and craniofacial defects as well as premature neurogenesis and neuronal delamination.
source: Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of Notch results in proximal PA and craniofacial defects as well as premature neurogenesis and neuronal delamination (Humphreys et al., 2012; Zuniga et al., 2010; Daudet and Lewis, 2005; de la Pompa et al., 1997; Lassiter et al., 2010; Lassiter et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of Notch in the cranial placodes prevents both neurogenesis and delamination and expands the placodal epithelium.
source: Conversely, activation of Notch in the cranial placodes prevents both neurogenesis and delamination and expands the placodal epithelium (Jayasena et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.
